mcqs.question: Why does stating your approach before typing code help even when the approach turns out to be correct?
options: It doesn't help when the approach is correct — it only matters when you're about to make a mistake
Stating the approach first is required by interview rules regardless of any real benefit
It mainly helps by giving the candidate more time to think while talking
It gives the interviewer something to evaluate immediately and a cheap chance to redirect a wrong turn in seconds instead of after minutes of typed code, on top of scoring communication directly
mcqs.explanation: Communication is graded on its own axis, and stating the plan first lets the interviewer redirect a wrong turn cheaply rather than after code is already written — both benefits apply even when the approach ends up correct. It's not a formality-only rule, and its main value isn't extra thinking time, it's the evaluation and redirection benefit.

mcqs.question: An interviewer asks "are you sure that handles duplicates?" and the candidate says "yeah I think so" and keeps coding unchanged. What's the risk?
options: The question was likely a deliberate signal that something is off, and not pausing to actually reconsider the approach reads as either missing the signal or not knowing how to act on it
There's no risk — verbally acknowledging the question is sufficient regardless of whether anything changes
The risk only applies if the candidate stays completely silent, not if they respond verbally at all
Pushback from an interviewer should always be dismissed unless it comes with an explicit correction
mcqs.explanation: Interviewer pushback is usually a deliberate, gentle signal, and acknowledging it verbally without actually pausing to reconsider reads just as badly as ignoring it silently — the missing step is genuinely re-evaluating, not just responding with words. A verbal reply alone doesn't neutralize the risk, and pushback shouldn't be dismissed by default.

mcqs.question: In a 45-minute round with two problems, why is spending 35 minutes perfecting the first problem's edge cases risky?
options: It's never risky — thoroughness on the first problem is always weighted more heavily than attempting a second one
It usually leaves too little time to attempt the second, likely harder problem at all, which typically costs more than a slightly rougher but complete first solution
The risk only applies if the candidate explicitly announces they're running out of time
Interviewers always extend the round automatically if the first problem takes longer than expected
mcqs.explanation: A round's time is usually budgeted across problems, and over-investing in the first one's polish often means running out the clock before the second is attempted at all, which tends to cost more overall than a good-enough first solution. Rounds aren't reliably extended, and the risk exists whether or not the candidate narrates their time usage.

mcqs.question: Why does building an abstract interface and multiple helper classes for a problem solvable with a fifteen-line loop often hurt rather than help?
options: It burns time better spent on correctness and testing, and mismatching solution complexity to problem complexity is often the opposite of the seniority signal it's meant to convey
It always helps, because more code structure is inherently viewed as more impressive regardless of problem size
It only hurts if the interviewer explicitly asks for the simplest possible solution
Abstraction is penalized only in phone screens, not in onsite rounds
mcqs.explanation: Over-engineering spends limited time on unneeded structure and tends to read as mismatched judgment rather than skill, since matching solution complexity to problem complexity is the actual senior signal. It isn't inherently impressive regardless of scale, it isn't conditioned on an explicit request for simplicity, and the risk applies in any round format.

mcqs.question: Why is a pre-interview self-check of these pitfalls useful even for a candidate who already knows the right algorithms?
options: It isn't useful — algorithm knowledge is the only thing that determines the outcome of a coding round
The self-check only matters for candidates who have never solved the specific problem before
These pitfalls are behavioral habits rather than knowledge gaps, so no amount of additional algorithm practice fixes them, and a short pre-round check catches them where practice alone wouldn't
It's useful only because interviewers explicitly grade whether a candidate ran a checklist beforehand
mcqs.explanation: These pitfalls sit on a behavioral axis separate from algorithm knowledge, so they persist regardless of how strong someone's technical prep is, and a quick self-check addresses exactly that gap. The outcome isn't determined by algorithm knowledge alone, the check isn't limited to unfamiliar problems, and interviewers aren't grading whether a checklist ritual happened.
